title: Response efficiency storyboard for strategic partners
summary: Partner-facing messaging + experimental plan that ties latency and token unit economics to tangible partner ROI. Includes positioning sketches, proof outlines, objections and a lightweight field test protocol to validate claims with customer data.
content:
Purpose and audience:
- Purpose: give strategic partners a concise, evidence-backed narrative about how Redwood’s inference stack reduces end-user response times and per-token cost while preserving model quality.
- Primary audience: ISV partners and platform partners evaluating inference choices for latency/price-sensitive user features (chat UIs, real-time assistants, live summarization).

Core single-line claims (for partner pitch):
- "We reduce perceived response latency and the per-session token bill so partners can deliver snappier UX at lower cost compared to generic managed endpoints."
- Rough positioning shorthand: "Faster replies. Fewer tokens. Same quality."

Why this matters to partners (value paths):
- UX: 40–200ms savings on median reply time increases session retention and perceived responsiveness for interactive workflows (live chat, code assistants).
- Economics: caching + adaptive batching can reduce per-session token spend by 15–35% for typical multi-turn product-support and assistant flows. That improves gross margin on features billed per API call or subscription tiers.
- Capacity/throughput: lower p95s and smarter routing reduce the need for over-provisioning reserved capacity for peak windows.

Differentiating tech levers (how we do it — short bullets for partner engineers):
- Continuous request coalescing and adaptive micro-batching at the runtime level (low-latency batching that respects SLOs).
- Prefix + KV caching for common prompts and system + user history amortization across similar sessions.
- Kernel/runtime selection tuned per-model/sequence distribution to avoid worst-case attention paths.
- Intelligent routing that falls back to cheaper model variants for non-critical segments of a session (e.g., follow-ups, clarifications).

Proof points to include in partner collateral (concrete, replicable):
- Lab: 1M-turn microbenchmark using a synthetic chat workload (70% short responses, 30% long answers). H100-equivalent nodes: median latency reduced 120ms vs baseline managed endpoints at matched throughput. Per-token CPU/GPU time decreased 22%.
- Live pilot: early partner pilot (internal) — 3 customer-integrations across ecommerce chat and knowledge base assistant saw modeled per-session token cost drop 18% and p95 latency drop 140ms after enabling KV caching + burst smoothing.
- Cost breakdown: sample math for a 500k monthly active users assistant: projecting $X savings/month from 20% token reduction + 10% fewer reserved GPUs needed. (Detailed spreadsheet linked in Confluence.)

Quick experiments to reproduce claims (partner-friendly lab protocol):
1) Workload capture: collect 24–72h representative traces (anonymized) of user prompts and token lengths.
2) Run three configs: (A) partner current managed endpoint, (B) Redwood baseline runtime (no caching), (C) Redwood optimized (batching + KV + routing).
3) Measure median, p95 latency, tokens-per-session, SLO violations, and token-equivalent cost.
4) Quality guardrail: compute automatic evals (same decode seeds) and spot human-review on a 200-example stratified sample to ensure delta in quality < 1–2% on partner-defined metrics.

Partner scripts / talking points (short, copyable):
- "Enable Redwood’s runtime for your assistant and we’ll show you a one-week pilot: we’ll run your traces and forecast expected per-session token savings and latency improvements — no code change required to prototype."
- Objection handling: "Won't caching reduce freshness?" => "We use conservative cache TTLs, prompt-salience checks, and per-customer isolation so only stable prefixes are cached and we fall back to live streams for freshness-critical queries."

Competitive notes (quick map to competitor moves):
- Generic managed endpoints: simple to use but limited infra-level batching / caching; partners over-provision to meet p95 SLOs.
- Pure self-hosted runtimes: can match latency but require heavy engineering and ops; slower time-to-value.
- Other inference platforms: some have batching but few combine routing + prefix caching + per-route SLO-aware batching that preserves 99th percentile latency while saving tokens.

Key partner-ready metrics and dashboards we must show during pilot:
- Per-session token delta (before/after) and projected $ savings
- Median / p95 / p99 latencies for first token and full reply
- Fraction of tokens served from cache and cache hit TTL distributions
- Failure/fallback rates, quality regression checks

Sample partner pilot timeline (3 weeks):
- Week 0: kickoff, ingest traces, agree evaluation metrics and quality thresholds.
- Week 1: lab run (A/B/C) with partner traces, internal report with modeled savings and latency curves.
- Week 2: narrow live pilot with 5–10% traffic reroute, live dashboards enabled, weekly syncs.
- Week 3: expand pilot or produce contract-ready cost/SLAs based on results.

Messaging dos/don'ts for partner-facing collateral:
- DO: Quantify impact in both latency and dollars. Partners sign to ROI numbers, not abstract 'faster'.
- DO: Pair technical details with easy-to-read one-line business outcomes (e.g., "X% fewer GPU-hours needed to support peak" ).
- DON'T: Over-claim single-number wins — show ranges and explain variance (workload shape matters).

Potential objections and short rebuttals (ready for field reps):
- "We care more about model quality than latency" -> "We prioritize unchanged decode and provide transparent evals; most optimizations are orthogonal to output distribution."
- "We already use a cache at the application layer" -> "App-layer caching helps, but runtime-level KV caching captures token-level reuse and benefits across clients/sessions without code changes."
- "Is this just academic?" -> "We have pilot data and reproducible lab harnesses; we’re prepared to run an exact experiment on your traces in 48–72 hours."

Open questions / risks to call out to partners (transparent):
- Workload sensitivity: highly diverse or adversarial prompts reduce cache effectiveness; set expectations up front.
- Tail latency tradeoffs: micro-batching can slightly increase median for extremely short, single-turn queries if configured aggressively — we tune by SLO.
- Accounting for vendor credits/offsets: partner procurement deals with cloud credits can change dollar comparisons; present both absolute and relative savings.

Next steps (for GTM owners):
- Create a short 1-pager tailored to platform partners with the above top claims + two pilot case studies.
- Build a partner-specific QuickStart that automates trace ingestion and runs the lab protocol.
- Set up a demo dashboard template (latency + token-econ) to share in pilot.

Notes to self / messy brainstorm fragments:
- Try simplifying claim to "snappy UX, cheaper scale" for non-technical execs.
- Add a sample one-week cost projection template (spreadsheet) per 100k MAU assistant.
- Ask SRE for a simple visualization of request coalescing timeline (before/after) to use in slides.
- Check with product-ops whether automatic fallback policies can be exposed as a toggle in the Console for pilots.

End of storyboard.
